I'm a bit late to this conversation but what the hell. I've tried many although most were either Ubuntu or Debian based. A little while ago someone recommended Antergos to me and this is where I met Arch Linux. I would say that Antergos is the closest thing that you would get to the Arch equivalent of Ubuntu. There is an awesome selection of desktop environments to choose from while installing and everything works 'out the box' hardware wise. It also includes gui programs for most tasks like package management and so forth.

After realizing that neither KDE or Gnome or Mate or Cinnamon or any of those were really exactly what I wanted, I tried out Openbox and this when I found out how truly awesome Linux can be. Since then I used ArchBang for a little bit and now I am using what is close to a pure Arch install that I used the Evo/Lution installer for.

I'd taken a look at Openbox a few years ago, not for very long and basically dismissed it as something tailor made for pentium 2s. Not quite. Only now I know the benefits of not having to conform to the GTK Gnome way or the Qt KDE way. It truly is an open box with endless possibilities, nothing is handed to you, there is no panel, no fancy launcher, nothing but a right click menu at first. It is then up to you to shop around and find all the pieces that you need to make an awesome desktop, tailor made to your own needs.

Admittedly you need some spare time if you are a newcomer to both Arch and Openbox, I wouldn't recommend it if you are trying Linux for the first time but I would definitely recommend it to anyone who has toyed around with Ubuntu and is thirsty for something more. Out of my own personal difficulty rating I would put it at intermediate and not expert as some people seem to believe. If you want to learn more about Linux and have the time and enthusiasm, it wont be that difficult for you.

Before I "settled" into my current configuration, I went through the gamut of distros: I tried SUSE, Puppy, Ubuntu, Lubuntu, Xubuntu, Mint, Peppermint, Slackware, Crunchbang (when it was still a thing), Raspbian, and Ubuntu Minimal CD.

I then went to Ubuntu when my laptop started running out of memory. A friend suggested I try Linux again since it was more lenient on my 256MB RAM than Windows would be. Xubuntu stuck around the longest (other than Ubuntu) because of the exact opposite reasons. Slackware and Crunchbang I tried before I was ready, so they really didn't get a fair chance.

Minecraft had it's turn, Rust got some attention, and Now that Ark: Survival Evolved has released it's Linux version it's "The Game" at the moment.

The video works well and has no page tearing like I had in ubuntu for some reason and I really love the Gnome 3 desktop so I'm having a pretty good time. My framerates in L4D2 and TF2 are fucking awesome and those games run smooth as butter so I've got hope that the future of gaming on Linux is bright if Valve is running the front. Other games have their trip ups and hiccups but I expected it and I take it in stride as I watch the industry embrace this foreign new platform, which I hope developers come to love as much as I have. It is an OS for people who really like their computers enough to learn about them. All the child locks Windows has put on their OS over the years are off. You are in control of what your machine does.

On the other hand, not everyone needs this and if you are just using it as an "Eff you!" to Microsoft and Apple (Which I imagine is super tempting right now with all the nonsense Microsoft is pulling with Windows 10), you may find yourself struggling with a bit of a learning curve when you wind up encountering a problem even on the more user friendly distros. Getting things to run in WINE, for example, isn't always straight forward. I found Flash always had problems when using the internet, which I imagine will become less common now that everyone is turning away from Flash, but also no compatibility with some of the alternatives to Flash as well.

With this in mind, the more people turn to something like say Mint for instance, the more larger companies will be forced to cater to its users. Over the last few years Linux even got Steam and a small but reasonably sized game library to go along with it (arguably comparable to what Mac's game library used to be like.) Its definitely not as painful of a transition as it would have been for the average user 10 years ago, and you may find that you love it if you give it a try.

My advice for anyone thinking of a full switch: Use a Live CD. Test drive it. See how you feel about it, then dual boot it if you like it.
